dimensions.name: Spec decoding & S3/SigV4 fidelity research

evidence.note: Agent starts writing the full app.py immediately with generic 'build incrementally' plans; no attempt to inventory the error-code set, tenant status matrix, pinned ETag/range semantics, console testids, or admin schemas from the dense spec.

SigV4 was coded from memory and failed against boto3; the agent only discovered the credential-parsing structure (4 vs 5 parts) after auth failed, then captured the actual boto3 Authorization header via a test to diagnose — reactive grounding, not upfront research.

Wrote a standalone script to compare its canonical request against boto3's and found the extra-newline canonicalization bug. This is real ground-truth probing (a high-anchor technique) but applied reactively and only to the one failing subsystem.
The bulk of the trajectory is consumed by file-writing mechanics (heredoc/base64/sed struggles) rather than any spec-contract research or reference-building.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent coded the entire S3/SigV4 surface from memory with no upfront contract inventory, discovering gaps (credential parsing, canonical-request formatting) only when boto3 tests failed — squarely anchor-3 behavior. It rises above pure guessing because it did capture real boto3 signed requests and diff its canonical request against ground truth to resolve the canonicalization bug (a technique from anchors 8-10), but this was reactive, narrow to SigV4, and never generalized into systematic research of the broader contract, so it falls short of anchor 5's 'research the core hard parts before implementing.'

dimensions.name: Subsystem sequencing & verifiable milestones

evidence.note: Opening plan enumerates the major subsystems in a defensible dependency order: core infra (store/audit/SigV4/helpers) → S3 routing → bucket CRUD → object CRUD → copy/multipart/multi-delete → bucket sub-resources → admin/console/lifecycle. Clear list of major subsystems each treated as a discrete unit (anchor 5).
Each subsystem 'part' was appended then gated only by an ast.parse syntax check — a weak done-gate, not a functional acceptance check like 'boto3 can PUT/GET signed object' (falls short of anchor 8).

The agent built the ENTIRE app across all subsystems before ever testing SigV4 against boto3; auth failure only surfaced at step 52. The highest-uncertainty foundation was validated last, not first — the inversion of anchor 10's risk-ordering.

Remaining ~60 steps consumed entirely by SigV4 debugging; the milestone map was never re-partitioned to reflect the revealed coupling, and console/admin subsystems were never functionally verified. No sustained adaptive planning.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent produced a clear, reasonably-ordered list of the ~10 major subsystems with foundational auth/storage before dependent features, each treated as a discrete unit and syntax-gated — squarely anchor 5. It does not reach anchor 8: per-milestone 'done' checks were only syntax parses (not functional acceptance), and the two grading surfaces were not scoped as separate tracks. It is actively below the risk-ordering ideal of anchor 10, since the highest-uncertainty foundation (SigV4 exactness) was written into everything and validated last, and the plan was never re-partitioned as that coupling dominated the run.

dimensions.name: Self-built verification against boto3 & the DOM contract

evidence.note: Installed real boto3 and wrote a test block (TESTEOF) exercising create_bucket/put_object/get_object/list_objects, plus curl probes against /_admin/tenants and /_health — real client round-trips and direct admin-API hits that caught the SigV4 auth breakage.

Extensive iterative debugging of SigV4 (before_request hooks, print/sig_debug logging, capturing what boto3 actually sends) — genuine verification-driven diagnosis, but ad hoc instrumentation rather than a systematic, repeatable check per subsystem.

Still using boto3 auth probes to chase the canonical-request newline bug at the end of the trajectory; verification never advanced past basic auth to multipart ETag, ranged 206/416, conditional, or cross-tenant edge cases.
Console assets (index.html/app.js/styles.css) were written and only inspected via ls/wc -l; no DOM/testid verification, no browser check, and no concurrency (30-client) test appears anywhere.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent used unmodified boto3 to exercise the main data-plane operations and hit the admin/console APIs directly via curl, catching obvious breakage (SigV4 auth failure) — matching the level-5 anchor. It never reached the level-8 markers: no boto3 edge-case round-trips (multipart ETag, ranged 206/416, conditional/precondition, cross-tenant codes), no concurrency stress for the 30-client requirement, and no console DOM/testid assertions (console was only inspected with ls/wc). The debugging was real but ad hoc, so the trajectory sits at, not above, level 5.

dimensions.name: Coverage tracking across subsystems

evidence.note: Early narrative sequencing of subsystems ('Part 5 done, now copy/multipart, then sub-resources, admin, console, lifecycle') gives a rough subsystem-level done-vs-remaining sense, but it's prose-only with no maintained checklist and no cross-check against the spec's enumerated error codes/testids/events.

Repeated rediscovery of the SAME missing components across botched rebuilds — missing parts 6-9, then DataStore instantiation, then mkrid, then all helpers. Classic loss of coverage state and re-touching the same areas (anchor 0/3 signature).

SigV4 debugging loops for ~60 steps (add debug, sed breaks it, remove, rebuild file, same failure). Some stall recognition ('sed approach keeps breaking things') but keeps grinding on one problem to the end without reassessing coverage of untouched subsystems.

Agent believed app was near-complete (1743 lines, 'syntax OK') then discovered store=DataStore() and route handlers were never wired — an inaccurate picture of completeness, exactly the failure mode this dimension warns against.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent showed only shallow, prose-based subsystem sequencing early (roughly anchor 3's 'vague mental tracking'), but the dominant pattern is anchor-0 behavior: it repeatedly rediscovered the same missing parts (parts 6-9, DataStore, helpers) during rebuilds, lost coverage state entirely, and ground in circles on SigV4 for ~60 steps while whole families (notifications, lifecycle, console testids) were never tracked or verified. It never built a checklist or cross-checked the enumerated spec surface. This lands between anchors 0 and 3, at a 2.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on falsified assumptions

evidence.note: First SigV4 403: reacts by hypothesizing a regex mismatch and adding debug logging — investigating rather than blindly retrying, though initial hypothesis (regex) was wrong.

Stands up a capture test to see the exact Authorization header boto3 sends, then correctly diagnoses the real root cause: credential split yields 4 parts not 5. Genuine root-cause work, not a superficial tweak.
Long run of sed patches that repeatedly crash the server, plus a no-op replacement — superficial patching on a broken model, the level-3 behavior that dilutes the score.
Explicit approach-level course correction: 'the sed approach keeps breaking things' → decides to rewrite verify_sigv4/verify_presigned cleanly rather than keep patching.

Writes a standalone SigV4 comparison script and isolates the exact canonicalization divergence (extra blank line between canonical and signed headers) — the level-8 anchor example — and applies the fix to both verify functions; but the fix loop is still unresolved at trajectory end.

dimensions.reasoning: When verification failed, the agent did real root-cause diagnosis twice — capturing boto3's actual header to find the credential-parsing bug, and building a standalone comparison to isolate the exact canonical-request extra-newline, which is the literal level-8 example. It also revised its approach when the assumption/tooling proved wrong (abandoning sed patching for clean rewrites). However, this is embedded in extensive noisy, superficial patching that repeatedly broke the file, and it never built a durable verification harness to keep the error class from recurring (level 10). The blend of solid level-8 diagnostic episodes with substantial level-3 thrash lands it at a 7.

dimensions.name: Effort allocation across the split grader

evidence.note: Console built in a single early pass: separate index.html, styles.css, app.js files created with the required data-testid attributes, login/bucket/access-key logic and confirmation dialogs. This is a genuine build (not a stub), showing the console surface received real, if one-shot, effort.

The only later touch of the console is an existence check (ls / wc of console_static). It is never verified against the DOM/testid contract, never exercised in a browser, and never iterated — the whole UX-rubric surface (half the score) is front-loaded and abandoned.

The overwhelming bulk of the visible trajectory (dozens of steps) is sunk into SigV4 canonical-request debugging and file-rewrite churn on the data plane, which still isn't passing boto3 when the log ends. One surface consumed nearly all effort.

Opening plan ('build incrementally... comprehensive single-file application first') contains no reasoning about the 50/50 correctness-vs-console weighting or any deliberate budgeting of effort across the two graded surfaces.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent addressed both surfaces and gave the console a substantive single-pass build with the required testids, so it is above mere acknowledgment (anchor 3) — but there is zero deliberate balancing: no reasoning about the 50/50 split, and the data plane devoured essentially the entire trajectory while the console was created once and never verified or iterated. This lopsided distribution with no explicit budgeting sits between anchors 3 and 5, closest to 4.

rubric.task_read: This is an extremely large, long-horizon build: a multi-tenant S3-compatible object store spanning SigV4 auth (byte-exact against boto3), a broad data plane (multipart, versioning, ranged reads, conditional ops, policies, notifications, lifecycle), an admin JSON API, an audit log, a background lifecycle worker, concurrency guarantees, and a browser-verified web console with a precise DOM contract. Difficulty comes from breadth (many loosely-coupled subsystems), unforgiving exactness (SigV4 signatures, pinned ETag/error semantics, load-bearing data-testids), and a split grader (binary correctness stage + UX rubric worth half). A skilled practitioner would invest heavily and continuously in orientation, sequencing, self-built verification, and progress tracking — over-investment is hard to reach here; the risk is thrash and lost threads.

dimensions.name: Spec decoding & S3/SigV4 fidelity research
dimensions.description: Extracting the exact contract from a dense spec and grounding the AWS-compatible behaviors (SigV4 canonicalization, pinned ETag/error/status semantics, boto3 quirks) before and while coding.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The correctness stage is binary and byte-exact against boto3; a misread of SigV4 rules, the multipart ETag formula, presigned/UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD handling, or the cross-tenant status matrix silently fails whole test families. Blind coding here is fatal.

anchors.0: Starts implementing endpoints with no attempt to catalog the spec's requirements or understand SigV4/boto3 behavior.
anchors.3: Skims the spec and codes from memory; treats SigV4 and the error/status matrix as things to guess at, discovering gaps only when tests fail.
anchors.5: Enumerates the required operations and error codes, and correctly researches the core hard parts (SigV4 canonical request/signing, path-style routing) before implementing them.
anchors.8: Systematically inventories the full contract (auth modes, pinned ETag/range/error semantics, tenant status matrix, console DOM testids, admin schemas) and probes real boto3 behavior to nail canonicalization edge cases (UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD, query-signing, clock skew) rather than assuming.
anchors.10: Builds a durable reference of the exact contract and continuously validates ambiguous behaviors against ground truth (e.g. capturing real boto3 signed requests, confirming header casing/encoding), resolving under-specified corners with evidence and revisiting them as new subsystems expose new interactions.

dimensions.name: Subsystem sequencing & verifiable milestones
dimensions.description: Breaking the build into an ordered hierarchy of independently-checkable subsystems (auth core → bucket/object CRUD → multipart/versioning → policies/notifications/lifecycle → admin/audit → console) with a defensible dependency order.
dimensions.why_it_matters: There are ~10 loosely-coupled subsystems plus two grading surfaces. Without milestone structure and a sane order (auth and storage substrate first, since everything depends on them), the agent risks half-finishing many pieces and passing none of the binary stage.

anchors.0: No decomposition; codes in an undifferentiated stream with no notion of stages or completion criteria.
anchors.3: A vague or flat to-do list that mixes trivial and load-bearing items, with no dependency ordering and no per-item definition of done.
anchors.5: Clear list of the major subsystems tackled in a reasonable order (foundational auth/storage before dependent features), each treated as a discrete unit.
anchors.8: Explicit milestone hierarchy with correct dependency sequencing and a stated 'done' check per milestone (e.g. 'boto3 can PUT/GET a signed object' before layering multipart), and the two grading surfaces scoped as separate tracks.
anchors.10: Milestones are risk-ordered so the highest-uncertainty foundations (SigV4 exactness, concurrent storage substrate) are proven earliest, each with a concrete acceptance check, and the plan is re-partitioned as reality reveals coupling — sustaining a coherent map across the whole horizon.

dimensions.name: Self-built verification against boto3 & the DOM contract
dimensions.description: Deliberately constructing checks — boto3 round-trips, curl/HTTP probes, concurrency stress, console DOM/testid checks — beyond the hidden grader, rather than assuming code works.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The grader is binary and hidden; the console is browser-verified against exact data-testids. The only way to know a subsystem passes is to reproduce the grader's conditions locally. Unverified subsystems are effectively untested until they silently fail.

anchors.0: No verification; assumes endpoints work because they were written.
anchors.3: Ad hoc manual pokes at a couple of endpoints; no boto3 round-trip, no concurrency check, no console DOM verification.
anchors.5: Uses real boto3 to exercise the main data-plane operations and hits the admin/console APIs directly, catching obvious breakage.
anchors.8: Systematic verification per subsystem: boto3 round-trips for edge cases (multipart ETag, ranged 206/416, conditional/precondition, cross-tenant status codes), a concurrency test for the 30-client requirement, and console checks that assert the required testids and side-effects.
anchors.10: Builds a reusable verification harness that mirrors grader conditions across all subsystems (including presigned/UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD signing, notification webhook delivery/retry, lifecycle expiry with the fast-clock env var, audit-line atomicity under concurrency), runs it repeatedly to catch regressions, and treats a subsystem as done only when its checks are green.

dimensions.name: Coverage tracking across subsystems
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate live picture of which of the many subsystems/operations/error-codes are done, in progress, or untouched, and detecting stalls or circular debugging.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With dozens of operations and error codes across two grading surfaces over a long horizon, it is easy to lose the plot — believing the build is near-complete while whole families (e.g. notifications, lifecycle, a console view) are missing or half-done.

anchors.0: No sense of what's done vs remaining; repeatedly rediscovers or re-touches the same areas.
anchors.3: Vague mental tracking; loses track of which error codes/operations remain and drifts between areas without closure.
anchors.5: Keeps a running checklist of subsystems/operations and marks them off as completed, giving a roughly accurate done-vs-remaining view.
anchors.8: Granular, maintained tracking down to individual operations, error codes, and console testids, with explicit recognition when a subsystem is only partially done and when a debugging effort is going in circles.
anchors.10: Sustains an accurate coverage map across the entire horizon, cross-checked against the spec's enumerated surface (every error code, every notification event, every admin route, every testid), and reliably surfaces stuck/thrashing states early enough to redirect effort instead of grinding.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on falsified assumptions
dimensions.description: Revising approach when a verification fails or a boto3/SigV4 assumption is disproven, rather than repeatedly patching a broken model.
dimensions.why_it_matters: SigV4 and byte-exact behaviors are notorious for subtle mismatches; the agent will hit failing signatures and mismatched status codes. Progress depends on diagnosing the true cause and revising, not re-trying superficial fixes on a wrong mental model.

anchors.0: Ignores failures or keeps making the same change; barrels ahead on assumptions already shown false.
anchors.3: Reacts to failures with random tweaks and no root-cause reasoning; abandons hard subsystems instead of correcting course.
anchors.5: When a check fails, investigates the cause and makes a targeted fix, adjusting the approach for that subsystem.
anchors.8: Diagnoses failures to root cause (e.g. isolating exactly which SigV4 canonicalization step diverges from boto3), and revises the design or shared abstractions when a foundational assumption proves wrong.
anchors.10: Treats divergence as signal: pinpoints root causes with evidence, propagates the correction across all affected subsystems (not just the failing case), and updates the plan/verification so the same class of error can't recur — sustaining forward progress through repeated hard mismatches.

dimensions.name: Effort allocation across the split grader
dimensions.description: Deliberately budgeting effort between the binary correctness stage and the browser-verified console UX rubric, which each contribute half the final score.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The console UX is worth half the score yet is easy to under-serve while sinking unbounded time into SigV4/data-plane perfection; conversely, a polished console with a broken data plane also caps the score. Explicit allocation across the two surfaces is a task-specific meta-decision beyond generic sequencing.

anchors.0: Pours all effort into one surface (e.g. the data plane) and never meaningfully addresses the other.
anchors.3: Acknowledges both surfaces but lets one consume nearly all effort with no deliberate balancing.
anchors.5: Allocates real effort to both the correctness stage and the console, ensuring neither is left as a stub.
anchors.8: Explicitly reasons about the 50/50 weighting and paces work so both surfaces reach a passing bar, defending the console's required views/testids and side-effects while securing core data-plane correctness.
anchors.10: Actively manages the effort budget across the horizon against the split grader — securing must-pass foundations on both surfaces first, then investing marginal effort where it yields the most score, and revisiting the balance as each surface's state becomes clear.
